title: The false cry
hookLine: a demon cries out in Rama's voice; only Lakshmana sees through it
carry: viveka: telling the real from the fake
tomorrow: Sita is alone now. who walks out of the trees?
last: MAYA DAZZLES, AND ISN'T WHAT IT SEEMS.

lines: A DYING SHOUT, IN RAMA'S VOICE.
cards: The arrow hits. The golden deer falls, and as it dies, it changes. The gold drains away, and there on the ground is Maricha, a huge rakshasa, just as Lakshmana said.
But Maricha has one last job. With his dying breath he shouts, and the voice that comes out is Rama's. Exactly Rama's, crying out in pain.
Oh Sita! Oh Lakshmana! Rama goes cold, turns, and runs for home.
And back at the hut, far away through the trees, Sita hears her husband's voice crying for help.

teach.b: Sita turns to Lakshmana: go! He's hurt! Lakshmana doesn't move.
Rama told him to guard her, whatever happened, and he knows his brother. Nobody in the three worlds can defeat Rama, he says. That cry is the demon, using his voice.
I'm staying. Sita, wild with fear, says the worst things she can think of. In Valmiki she accuses Lakshmana of wanting Rama dead, even of wanting her for himself.
Lakshmana, who gave up everything to follow them, is stung to the core, and he goes.
Yesterday you met maya: something that dazzles and isn't what it seems. First a golden deer, now a perfect voice.
Hindu teachers have a name for what answers maya: viveka, discernment, telling the real from the unreal. In Advaita Vedanta it's the first of four qualities a seeker needs. Lakshmana has it here.
He hears the cry as clearly as Sita does, but he holds it up against what he knows is true: Rama can't be beaten. Sita can't, because the fake was built out of her love.

Many teachers read the scene this way: maya never looks false. It looks like the thing you love most, in trouble, right now, and it wants you moving before you think. The tradition doesn't blame Sita alone.
It shows how fast fear turns two loyal people against each other. Today the false cry might be a text saying someone you love is hurt, or a call in a voice you'd know anywhere, asking for money now.

teach.h: VIVEKA: TELLING THE REAL FROM THE FAKE.
teach.b: Viveka is Lakshmana's pause: is this real?

how: Hindus retell the scene of the false cry as a warning about deception and fear; teachers often read Maricha's deer and voice as maya and Lakshmana's calm as viveka, discernment, which many Hindus pray for each morning in the Gayatri.

o: a war cry Rama gives as the deer falls
Maricha's dying shout, faked in Rama's voice
Rama's real call for help, deep in the woods

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: a master of maya: first a deer, then a voice
something that dazzles and isn't what it seems
telling the real from the unreal
nobody can defeat Rama. it's a trick.

s: the voice Sita hears is really Rama's
it's Maricha, dying, imitating Rama perfectly. maya at work.
maya means something that obviously looks fake
maya convinces. the false cry sounded exactly like Rama, in trouble.
Lakshmana first refuses to leave Sita
he knows the cry is a trick, and Rama told him to guard her. he goes only when her words sting him.

games.q: a voice message arrives that sounds exactly like your cousin, crying, saying they're in trouble and need money right now. what would Lakshmana's viveka do?
o: send it fast. it sounds exactly like them.
pause and check what's true: call them back on the number you know.
decide every scary message is fake from now on.
games.why: viveka isn't doubting everything. it's holding a voice up against what you know is true, before fear moves you.

practice: On day three you learned the Gayatri, the prayer for a clear mind. Many Hindus say it every morning, and its last line asks the divine light to wake up and guide our minds. Say that line now, slowly: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat.
If you don't pray, say its meaning instead. Then hold up one message that once made you panic, and ask it Lakshmana's question: what do I know is true?

wordCard.voice: The cry. Maricha's last trick: a dying shout in Rama's voice. Lakshmana heard it for what it was.

orig.note: Sanskrit: voice, sound, tone; Maricha's dying cry in Rama's voice.

carryVoice: Carry this: viveka, telling the real from the fake. Lakshmana's was the quiet voice. That's fifty days in.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 44–45 (Maricha's death and cry; Sita and Lakshmana)
Advaita Vedanta: viveka, first of the four qualifications of a seeker (sadhana chatushtaya), as taught in the school of Shankara
Rig Veda 3.62.10 (the Gayatri mantra; its last line asks that our minds be stirred and guided)
